months.name: January
months.intro: A new year starts with a simple sorting job. Some things belong to you: your judgments, your choices, the effort you bring. Most things do not: other people, the weather, the economy, your reputation. This month practices telling the two apart, and putting your energy where it can actually do some good.

entries.title: Two Kinds of Things
entries.quote: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, turning from a thing; and in a word, whatever are our acts.
entries.reflection: Start the year by drawing one line down the middle of your life. On one side sit your opinions, wants and actions. On the other sit the stock market, your boss's mood and the flu going around the office. Most stress comes from pushing hard on the wrong side of that line and wondering why nothing moves.
entries.practice: Write two columns tonight, mine and not mine, and sort three current worries into them.

entries.title: The Judgment, Not the Thing
entries.quote: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.
entries.reflection: A rude email arrives, and the sting feels like it came with the message. Look closer. The words are pixels on a screen; the hurt comes from the story you attach to them about respect, fairness or failure. That story is yours, which means it can be edited, softened or dropped before lunch.
entries.practice: When something annoys you today, name the judgment behind it in one short sentence.

entries.title: Pain and Opinion
entries.quote: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it; but if, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and say, “It is nothing,—a trifling matter at most; keep a stout heart and it will soon cease”; then in thinking it slight, you will make it slight. Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer.
entries.reflection: Seneca wrote this while managing real illness, so it is no casual pep talk. A sore back is a sore back. Yet the extra layer, the dread that it will never improve or that it ruins everything, is something the mind adds. Notice how much of a bad day is the commentary rather than the event.
entries.practice: Describe one discomfort today in plain facts only, leaving out every forecast and complaint.

entries.title: Free by Nature
entries.quote: And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint or hindrance; but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others.
entries.reflection: Nobody can stop you from deciding to be patient with a toddler or honest in a meeting. Those choices cannot be blocked. A promotion, a refund or a quick reply from a friend, however, sits in someone else's hands and can be delayed at any moment. Leaning your peace on the second kind invites a fragile week.
entries.practice: Pick one goal you hold and rewrite it so that success depends only on your effort.

entries.title: No Opinion Required
entries.quote: It is in our power to have no opinion about a thing, and not to be disturbed in our soul; for things themselves have no natural power to form our judgments.
entries.reflection: Not every event needs a verdict. The neighbor's new fence, a headline you scrolled past, a stranger's odd parking job: each one can simply be noticed and left alone. Forming an opinion feels automatic, but it is optional. Skipping a few of them frees up a surprising amount of attention for things that matter.
entries.practice: Let three small things pass today without judging them good or bad, even silently.

entries.title: Your Own Verdict
entries.quote: However, what you think of yourself is much more to the point than what others think of you.
entries.reflection: Likes, reviews and the quiet ranking of colleagues all shift with moods you cannot see. Your own honest assessment of how you lived today is steadier and closer to the truth. This is not about flattering yourself. It means grading yourself on standards you chose, instead of on applause that comes and goes.
entries.practice: Before bed, rate your day by one standard you chose, not by anyone's reaction.

entries.title: You Are an Appearance
entries.quote: Straightway then practise saying to every harsh appearance: You are an appearance, and in no manner what you appear to be.
entries.reflection: A frown from your spouse, a red number on a lab result, a late notice in the mail: each arrives looking like a verdict. Pausing to call it an impression buys a few seconds of space. In that gap you can check what it really means before your stomach decides for you.
entries.practice: When bad news lands today, say quietly, this is an impression, then take one breath.

entries.title: The Retreat Within
entries.quote: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
entries.reflection: Vacations are lovely, and the cabin by the lake will still be booked out for months. The calmer room is closer. A few slow minutes in the car before walking into the house, or at your desk between calls, can reset a frayed mind. That retreat is always open and costs nothing.
entries.practice: Take five quiet minutes in your parked car or at your desk before your next task.

entries.title: Passenger and Pilot
entries.quote: A pilot has a double rôle: one he shares with all his fellow-passengers, for he also is a passenger; the other is peculiar to him, for he is the pilot. The storm harms him as a passenger, but not as a pilot.
entries.reflection: Turbulence rattles everyone on the plane, including the person flying it. The difference is that the pilot still has a job to do while the cabin shakes. A layoff rumor or a family crisis may toss you around as a passenger. Your role as the one steering your own conduct stays fully intact.
entries.practice: In today's hardest moment, ask what the pilot in you should do next.

entries.title: An Impediment to the Leg
entries.quote: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.
entries.reflection: A torn ligament can cancel the running season. It cannot cancel kindness, curiosity or the choice to rehab with care. Illness and injury narrow what the body can do, and that loss is real. Yet the part of you that decides how to meet the setback remains unhurt and ready to work.
entries.practice: Name one limit you face and one choice that limit cannot touch.

entries.title: Let It Fall
entries.quote: Let there fall externally what will on the parts which can feel the effects of this fall. For those parts which have felt will complain, if they choose. But I, unless I think that what has happened is an evil, am not injured. And it is in my power not to think so.
entries.reflection: Rain on the commute, a dent in the bumper, a cold that lingers for a week. These land on the outer parts of life, and they may ache. Whether they also count as disasters is a separate question, and you get the final word on it. Many days improve once that word is withheld.
entries.practice: When a minor setback happens today, decline to call it bad for one full hour.

entries.title: Hope and Despair
entries.quote: You will of your own volition be sowing a crop of trouble by alternate hoping and despairing. If you are wise, mingle these two elements: do not hope without despair, or despair without hope.
entries.reflection: Waiting on test results, a job offer or a house closing can feel like riding a swing. Each email lifts or drops you. The swinging is self-made, because neither outcome is decided by your mood. Holding hope and realism together steadies the ride and leaves energy for the work that is actually yours.
entries.practice: Write down your best and worst realistic outcomes for one pending matter, then close the notebook.

entries.title: Keep What Is Yours
entries.quote: Keep by every means what is your own; do not desire what belongs to others. Fidelity (integrity) is your own, virtuous shame is your own; who then can take these things from you? who else than yourself will hinder you from using them?
entries.reflection: Your word, your decency and your sense of shame at a cheap shortcut belong only to you. A thief can take the car; nobody can take your integrity unless you hand it over. That handing over usually happens quietly, in a small fudge on a form or a promise left to slide.
entries.practice: Keep one small promise today that nobody would notice if you broke.

entries.title: Blame Nobody
entries.quote: Thou must blame nobody. For if thou canst, correct [that which is the cause]; but if thou canst not do this, correct at least the thing itself; but if thou canst not do even this, of what use is it to thee to find fault? for nothing should be done without a purpose.
entries.reflection: Blame feels productive, but it rarely fixes the leaking sink. When something goes wrong, the useful questions are simple. Can I fix the cause? If not, can I handle the result? If neither, then griping only adds a second problem to the first. This keeps attention on repair instead of on fault.
entries.practice: When something goes wrong today, ask only, what can I fix, before saying anything else.

entries.title: Ruled by Reason
entries.quote: Proceed with steady step, and if you would have all things under your control, put yourself under the control of reason; if reason becomes your ruler, you will become ruler over many.
entries.reflection: Wanting control over everything usually ends in exhaustion: the kids, the team, the traffic, the group chat. Seneca turns the wish around. Govern your own reactions first, and you will find you handle far more situations well. Steady people end up shaping rooms without trying to control them.
entries.practice: Before reacting to a frustration today, count to five and choose your response on purpose.

entries.title: What Will Happen?
entries.quote: What shall I do? how will it be? how will it turn out? will this happen? will that? All these are the words of those who are turning themselves to things which are not within the power of the will.
entries.reflection: Lying awake rehearsing tomorrow's meeting or next month's bills is a familiar habit. The questions keep circling because they aim at outcomes nobody can settle at three in the morning. A better question is smaller and answerable: what will I do, and how well will I do it?
entries.practice: Turn one nagging what-if into a single next action, and write it down.

entries.title: A Different Prayer
entries.quote: Another thus: How shall I not lose my little son? Thou thus: How shall I not be afraid to lose him?
entries.reflection: Every parent knows this fear, and Marcus lost several children, so he knew it too. He does not ask anyone to stop loving. He suggests asking for courage instead of guarantees. Nobody can promise that loved ones stay safe, but you can ask to meet whatever comes without being ruled by dread.
entries.practice: Replace one worried wish today with a request for the strength to handle it.

entries.title: Your Own Audience
entries.quote: O what ample matter were there for renown, if we could have spectators of our sickness! Be your own spectator; seek your own applause.
entries.reflection: Some of the bravest work happens where nobody sees it: a sick day handled without snapping, a caregiving night, a quiet apology. No one posts about those. Seneca suggests that your own approval is enough witness. Doing well with no audience may be the clearest sign you are acting for the right reasons.
entries.practice: Do one good thing today and tell no one about it.

entries.title: We Squeeze Ourselves
entries.quote: For remember this general truth, that it is we who squeeze ourselves, who put ourselves in straits; that is, our opinions squeeze us and put us in straits.
entries.reflection: A packed calendar, a crowded kitchen, a tight budget can all feel like walls closing in. Often the real pressure comes from the opinion that everything must happen now and perfectly. Loosen that belief and the same room tends to feel bigger, even before anything on the schedule changes.
entries.practice: Find one self-imposed rule that is squeezing you today and relax it.

entries.title: The Promontory
entries.quote: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.
entries.reflection: Waves keep coming: complaints, deadlines, the endless ping of notifications. A rocky headland does not argue with the sea or try to stop the tide. It simply holds its shape, and the water calms around it. Your steadiness can work the same way for a tense household or office.
entries.practice: In your next tense conversation, lower your voice and slow your speech on purpose.

entries.title: Fortune's Full Reach
entries.quote: Meanwhile, hold fast to this thought, and grip it close: yield not to adversity; trust not to prosperity; keep before your eyes the full scope of Fortune’s power, as if she would surely do whatever is in her power to do.
entries.reflection: Good years tempt you to assume they will last, and bad ones tempt you to assume they never end. Both assumptions hand your calm to chance. Keeping in mind that circumstances can turn either way is not gloomy. It lets you enjoy a raise or survive a loss without being knocked off balance.
entries.practice: Name one good thing you assume will last, and thank it as if it might not.

entries.title: Like a Stone
entries.quote: Stand by a stone and revile it, and what will you gain? If then a man listens like a stone, what profit is there to the reviler?
entries.reflection: An insult needs a landing spot. When a driver honks or a commenter sneers, the barb only works if you catch it and hold on. Listening calmly, without taking the bait, leaves the critic with nothing to push against. Useful feedback can still be kept; the venom can be left on the curb.
entries.practice: When someone takes a jab at you today, answer calmly or not at all.

entries.title: Let Them Be Liars
entries.quote: Let it not be in any man's power to say truly of thee that thou are not simple or that thou art not good; but let him be a liar whoever shall think anything of this kind about thee; and this is altogether in thy power.
entries.reflection: Gossip and criticism are out of your hands. Whether they are accurate is not. If you live honestly and kindly, a false remark stays false no matter how loudly it travels. That shifts the job from managing your image, which is impossible, to managing your conduct, which is entirely possible.
entries.practice: Pick one quality you want said of you, and act on it once before noon.

entries.title: A Safe Harbour
entries.quote: The only harbour safe from the seething storms of this life is scorn of the future, a firm stand, a readiness to receive Fortune’s missiles full in the breast, neither skulking nor turning the back.
entries.reflection: Worrying about next year's economy, next week's diagnosis or tomorrow's commute rarely prepares you for any of them. A firmer stance helps more: decide now to face whatever comes rather than flinch from it. Readiness of that kind is a habit you can build, and it travels well.
entries.practice: Choose one thing you dread and decide exactly how you will face it.

entries.title: Who Can Compel You?
entries.quote: If you choose to be modest and faithful, who shall not allow you to be so? If you choose not to be restrained or compelled, who shall compel you to desire what you think that you ought not to desire? who shall compel you to avoid what you do not think fit to avoid?
entries.reflection: Pressure can shape your options, but it cannot reach inside and pick for you. A pushy salesperson, a group of friends ordering another round, a manager hinting at a shortcut: none of them can force your agreement. The final yes or no stays in your mouth, even when saying it is hard.
entries.practice: Say no today to one request that goes against what you actually value.

entries.title: Your Own Good
entries.quote: He who loves fame considers another man's activity to be his own good; and he who loves pleasure, his own sensations; but he who has understanding considers his own acts to be his own good.
entries.reflection: If your happiness depends on praise, you have parked it in other people's mouths. If it depends on pleasure, it rides on sensations that fade by dinner. Measuring a day by what you did well puts the scorecard back in your own hands, where nobody else can smudge it.
entries.practice: Tonight list three things you did well today, regardless of how anyone responded.

entries.title: Ready for Either
entries.quote: He is ready for either outcome: if it brings goods, he controls them; if evils, he conquers them. So thoroughly, I mean, has he schooled himself that he makes manifest his virtue in prosperity as well as in adversity, and keeps his eyes on virtue itself, not on the objects with which virtue deals.
entries.reflection: A good quarter and a bad one both test character. Money can make you careless, and loss can make you bitter. Paying attention to how you behave, rather than to which way things broke, keeps you useful in both. The circumstances change; the job of acting well stays the same.
entries.practice: Whatever news arrives today, ask how a person you admire would carry it.

entries.title: Contend With the Image
entries.quote: Then, when the appearance (of things) pains you, for it is not in your power to prevent this, contend against it by the aid of reason, conquer it: do not allow it to gain strength nor to lead you to the consequences by raising images such as it pleases and as it pleases.
entries.reflection: A first jolt of hurt or fear arrives on its own, and that part is not your fault. What follows is different. One painful thought can spawn ten imagined scenes of worse to come. Catching that chain early, and refusing to let it run, is where your real power begins.
entries.practice: When a painful thought arrives, stop at the first image and refuse the sequel.

entries.title: The Citadel
entries.quote: Therefore the mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure to which he can fly for refuge and for the future be inexpugnable.
entries.reflection: Houses, savings and health can all be breached by events. A settled mind is harder to storm. It does not mean feeling nothing; it means not being dragged around by every surge of anger or fear. Building that inner fortress happens in ordinary moments, one calm response at a time.
entries.practice: Notice the next surge of anger today and wait ten breaths before acting on it.

entries.title: Goods From Within
entries.quote: Accordingly, let your thoughts, your efforts, your desires, help to make you content with your own self and with the goods that spring from yourself; and commit all your other prayers to God’s keeping!
entries.reflection: Wishing for a bigger house, a better job or a smoother family is natural. Seneca suggests sending those wishes off and turning your effort toward what grows from you: patience, skill, generosity. Those goods are portable and cannot be repossessed, which makes them a surprisingly secure investment.
entries.practice: Spend twenty minutes today improving one skill that nobody can take away from you.

entries.title: A Waveless Bay
entries.quote: Consider that everything is opinion, and opinion is in thy power. Take away then, when thou choosest, thy opinion, and like a mariner who has doubled the promontory, thou wilt find calm, everything stable, and a waveless bay.
entries.reflection: After a month of sorting what is yours from what is not, one tool stands out. Your opinions are the rudder. Change how you judge a delay, a loss or a slight, and the rough water often calms. The sea may stay choppy, yet the ship feels steadier.
entries.practice: Review this month's two-column list and move any worry that belongs in the other column.

months.name: February
months.intro: Anger, fear, grief and desire are not enemies to be crushed; they are weather that moves through every life. This month is about noticing them early, feeling them honestly, and keeping your hands on the wheel while they pass. The goal is not a colder heart but a steadier one.

entries.title: Catch It Small
entries.quote: Every emotion at the start is weak. Afterwards, it rouses itself and gains strength by progress; it is more easy to forestall it than to forgo it.
entries.reflection: Irritation at a slow reply, a flicker of envy at a friend's new house, a small worry about a test result. Each starts as a spark you could pinch out with two fingers. Wait an hour, feed it with replayed conversations, and it becomes a fire that runs your evening. Noticing early is most of the work.
entries.practice: When you feel the first twinge of irritation today, name it out loud and pause.

entries.title: Back in Tune
entries.quote: When thou hast been compelled by circumstances to be disturbed in a manner, quickly return to thyself, and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts; for thou wilt have more mastery over the harmony by continually recurring to it.
entries.reflection: Nobody stays calm all the time, and Marcus does not ask you to. A bad phone call or a near miss on the highway will knock you off balance. What matters is how quickly you come back. Like a musician retuning between songs, the more often you return to center, the easier the return becomes.
entries.practice: After any upsetting moment today, take three slow breaths before your next action.

entries.title: Sympathy Without Drowning
entries.quote: When you see a person weeping in sorrow either when a child goes abroad or when he is dead, or when the man has lost his property, take care that the appearance do not hurry you away with it, as if he were suffering in external things. But straightway make a distinction in your own mind, and be in readiness to say, it is not that which has happened that afflicts this man, for it does not afflict another, but it is the opinion about this thing which afflicts the man.
entries.reflection: When a friend calls in tears about a layoff or a diagnosis, it is easy to get swept into the same panic. Real help usually needs a steadier person on the line. You can grieve with someone while remembering that their pain flows from how they see the event, and that a calm view may help them most.
entries.practice: When someone shares bad news today, listen fully before offering any reaction or advice.

entries.title: No Bread Tonight
entries.quote: So I am getting rid of fatigue at my writing-table: I derive some good from this tardiness on the part of my cook and my baker. For I am communing with myself on this very topic—that nothing is heavy if one accepts it with a light heart, and that nothing need provoke one’s anger if one does not add to one’s pile of troubles by getting angry.
entries.reflection: Seneca arrives home tired, finds dinner unready, and decides to treat it as a lesson rather than an outrage. Most of our anger works this way: the late delivery or the forgotten errand is small, and the fury we pile on top is what makes it heavy. Taking it lightly is a choice, not a personality.
entries.practice: When something at home goes wrong today, describe it once in plain words, then let it go.

entries.title: The Bitter Honey
entries.quote: To the jaundiced honey tastes bitter, and to those bitten by mad dogs water causes fear; and to little children the ball is a fine thing. Why then am I angry? Dost thou think that a false opinion has less power than the bile in the jaundiced or the poison in him who is bitten by a mad dog?
entries.reflection: A sick tongue makes good honey taste foul, and a mistaken belief makes ordinary events feel like insults. When a coworker's short email ruins your morning, the email may not be the real problem. Your reading of it might be. Asking why you are angry often reveals an opinion you can examine and revise.
entries.practice: Before reacting to any message that annoys you, write down what you assumed it meant.

entries.title: Who Holds Your Mind
entries.quote: If any person was intending to put your body in the power of any man whom you fell in with on the way, you would be vexed; but that you put your understanding in the power of any man whom you meet, so that if he should revile you, it is disturbed and troubled, are you not ashamed at this?
entries.reflection: You would never hand your car keys to a stranger in a parking lot. Yet a rude driver, an anonymous comment, or a snippy relative can take control of your mood for hours. Their words are theirs. Whether those words get to steer your thoughts is still up to you, and that is worth guarding carefully.
entries.practice: If someone insults or criticizes you today, wait ten minutes before you reply.

entries.title: Hope and Fear Together
entries.quote: Just as the same chain fastens the prisoner and the soldier who guards him, so hope and fear, dissimilar as they are, keep step together; fear follows hope. I am not surprised that they proceed in this way; each alike belongs to a mind that is in suspense, a mind that is fretted by looking forward to the future.
entries.reflection: Hoping hard for the promotion, the clean scan, or the perfect vacation quietly creates its twin, the dread that it will not happen. Both live in a future that has not arrived. Loosening your grip on outcomes does not mean you stop caring. It means today stops being held hostage by tomorrow.
entries.practice: Notice one hope you keep checking on today, and turn your attention to the present task.

entries.title: Ask Instead of Fearing
entries.quote: What need is there of suspicious fear, since it is in thy power to inquire what ought to be done? And if thou seest clear, go by this way content, without turning back; but if thou dost not see clear, stop and take the best advisers.
entries.reflection: Vague dread thrives on not looking. The unopened bill, the odd noise in the engine, the tension with a sibling all grow larger in the dark. Marcus points to a simpler move: find out what needs doing. If the path is clear, take it. If it is not, ask someone who knows more than you.
entries.practice: Pick one thing you have been avoiding out of worry and take the first concrete step.

entries.title: Knowing What You Hold
entries.quote: If you love an earthen vessel, say it is an earthen vessel which you love; for when it has been broken you will not be disturbed. If you are kissing your child or wife, say that it is a human being whom you are kissing, for when the wife or child dies you will not be disturbed.
entries.reflection: This sounds harsh at first, but it is really about honesty. A favorite mug can break. The people you love are mortal. Remembering this does not make you love them less; it can make the goodnight hug or the ordinary dinner feel more precious, and it softens the shock when loss eventually comes.
entries.practice: Tonight, give the people at home your full attention for one uninterrupted conversation.

entries.title: Let the Tears Fall
entries.quote: Tears fall, no matter how we try to check them, and by being shed they ease the soul. What, then, shall we do? Let us allow them to fall, but let us not command them do so; let us weep according as emotion floods our eyes, but not as much as mere imitation shall demand. Let us, indeed, add nothing to natural grief, nor augment it by following the example of others.
entries.reflection: Stoicism is often mistaken for a stiff upper lip. Seneca disagrees. Grief that rises on its own deserves to be felt, and tears can bring real relief. What he warns against is performing sorrow for an audience or feeding it beyond its natural course. Honest feeling, without the extra layers of show.
entries.practice: If something saddens you today, allow yourself to feel it privately for a few minutes.

entries.title: Go Away, Thought
entries.quote: What then art thou doing here, O imagination? Go away, I entreat thee by the gods, as thou didst come, for I want thee not. But thou art come according to thy old fashion. I am not angry with thee: only go away.
entries.reflection: Old worries and resentments return like a neighbor who knocks at the same hour each night. Marcus does not scold the thought or fight it. He simply tells it to leave, without anger. The next time a familiar anxious loop starts at two in the morning, a gentle refusal may work better than an argument.
entries.practice: When a recurring worry shows up today, quietly say not now, and return to your task.

entries.title: The Stolen Coat
entries.quote: Why then are we angry? Is it because we value so much the things of which these men rob us? Do not admire your clothes, and then you will not be angry with the thief.
entries.reflection: Much of our anger at others tracks how much we prize what they took or damaged. A dented bumper enrages the person who treats the car as part of their identity. Valuing things a little less does not make you careless. It makes the inevitable scratches, losses, and thefts far easier to absorb.
entries.practice: Identify one possession you guard anxiously, and imagine calmly how you would cope without it.

entries.title: Fear of Losing
entries.quote: It is tragic for the soul to be apprehensive of the future and wretched in anticipation of wretchedness, consumed with an anxious desire that the objects which give pleasure may remain in its possession to the very end. For such a soul will never be at rest; in waiting for the future it will lose the present blessings which it might enjoy. And there is no difference between grief for something lost and the fear of losing it.
entries.reflection: Sometimes the fear of losing something does more damage than the loss itself. Parents who constantly imagine harm to their children, or savers who check the market every hour, suffer the loss in advance and again if it ever arrives. Meanwhile the good thing sitting right in front of them goes unenjoyed.
entries.practice: Spend fifteen minutes enjoying something you value without checking on its future.

entries.title: Turn the Mirror
entries.quote: When thou art offended at any man's fault, forthwith turn to thyself and reflect in what like manner thou dost err thyself; for example, in thinking that money is a good thing, or pleasure, or a bit of reputation, and the like. For by attending to this thou wilt quickly forget thy anger, if this consideration also is added, that the man is compelled: for what else could he do? or, if thou art able, take away from him the compulsion.
entries.reflection: Your colleague takes credit for your work, and the irritation flares. Before it hardens, ask where you have chased status, money, or approval in your own way. Seeing the same weakness in yourself rarely excuses the behavior, but it cools the outrage and leaves you clearer about how to respond.
entries.practice: The next time someone annoys you, recall one time you made a similar mistake.

entries.title: Let It Wait
entries.quote: If you have received the impression of any pleasure, guard yourself against being carried away by it; but let the thing wait for you, and allow yourself a certain delay on your own part. Then think of both times, of the time when you will enjoy the pleasure, and of the time after the enjoyment of the pleasure, when you will repent and will reproach yourself.
entries.reflection: The urge to order dessert, buy the gadget, or scroll for another twenty minutes always feels urgent. Epictetus suggests a simple delay. Picture the moment of enjoyment, then picture yourself afterward. Often the second picture settles the matter, and the craving loses its grip once you have given it a pause.
entries.practice: Before your next impulse purchase or snack, wait five minutes and picture how you will feel after.

entries.title: Subtract, Don't Add
entries.quote: “If you wish,” said he, “to make Pythocles rich, do not add to his store of money, but subtract from his desires.”
entries.reflection: The usual plan for feeling richer is to earn more. Epicurus, quoted here by Seneca, offers the other lever: want less. A raise can be swallowed by rising expectations, but trimming a desire works immediately and costs nothing. Contentment often arrives faster by subtraction than by any amount of addition.
entries.practice: Cancel or skip one purchase or subscription you only half want.

entries.title: One Letter at a Time
entries.quote: Just so then in this life also remember that every duty is made up of certain parts. These it is thy duty to observe, and without being disturbed or showing anger towards those who are angry with thee, to go on thy way and finish that which is set before thee.
entries.reflection: When the people around you are tense, their mood can tug you into the same storm. A meeting turns sharp, a child melts down, a customer raises their voice. The steady path is to keep doing the next small part of your job well, without matching the heat that others bring into the room.
entries.practice: When someone around you gets heated today, lower your voice and focus on the next step.

entries.title: The Missing Lamp
entries.quote: I also lately had an iron lamp placed by the side of my household gods; hearing a noise at the door, I ran down, and found that the lamp had been carried off. I reflected that he who had taken the lamp had done nothing strange. What then? To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp; for a man only loses that which he has.
entries.reflection: Epictetus loses a lamp to a thief and responds with a shrug and a cheaper replacement. The thief did what thieves do. You only lose what you own, so ownership always carries the chance of loss. Seeing that ahead of time turns a stolen package or broken phone into an errand rather than a tragedy.
entries.practice: If something breaks or goes missing today, replace or repair it without telling the story twice.

entries.title: Twice Tormented
entries.quote: Beasts avoid the dangers which they see, and when they have escaped them are free from care; but we men torment ourselves over that which is to come as well as over that which is past. Many of our blessings bring bane to us; for memory recalls the tortures of fear, while foresight anticipates them.
entries.reflection: A deer escapes the hawk and goes back to grazing. People replay last year's embarrassment and rehearse next month's disaster in the same afternoon. Memory and imagination are gifts, but they can also make you live through pain that is long over or may never come. Present trouble is usually enough.
entries.practice: When you catch yourself replaying an old regret, stand up and do something with your hands.

entries.title: Check the Strings
entries.quote: Perceive at last that thou hast in thee something better and more divine than the things which cause the various affects, and as it were pull thee by the strings. What is there now in my mind,—is it fear, or suspicion, or desire, or anything of the kind?
entries.reflection: Feelings can pull you around like a puppet: a notification jolts you, a headline sours you, a craving steers you to the fridge. Marcus asks a plain question worth borrowing. What is in my mind right now? Naming the fear, suspicion, or desire is often enough to loosen its hold on your hands.
entries.practice: Three times today, stop and ask yourself which feeling is steering you right now.

entries.title: Small Change First
entries.quote: Begin then from little things. Is the oil spilled? Is a little wine stolen? Say on the occasion, at such price is sold freedom from perturbation; at such price is sold tranquillity, but nothing is got for nothing.
entries.reflection: Nobody learns calm in a crisis. You practice on spilled coffee, a lost charger, a child who left the milk out. Each small annoyance is a cheap lesson in letting go. Pay that small price now, and you build the habit that will hold when something truly hard arrives.
entries.practice: Treat the first minor mishap today as practice and respond with deliberate calm.

entries.title: Remembering Without Bitterness
entries.quote: You may, however, speak often concerning the departed, and cherish his memory to the extent of your power. This memory will return to you all the more often if you welcome its coming without bitterness; for no man enjoys converse with one who is sorrowful, much less with sorrow itself.
entries.reflection: Grief does not require silence. Seneca encourages talking about the people you have lost and keeping their memory close. The difference lies in tone. Memories approached with gratitude keep visiting gladly; memories wrapped in bitterness become painful to touch, and so they fade. Let the stories be warm.
entries.practice: Share one happy memory of someone you have lost with a friend or family member.

entries.title: Feel It, Don't Judge It
entries.quote: Let the part of thy soul which leads and governs be undisturbed by the movements in the flesh, whether of pleasure or of pain; and let it not unite with them, but let it circumscribe itself and limit those affects to their parts.
entries.reflection: A sore back, a craving, a rush of adrenaline before a hard conversation are all real sensations in the body. Marcus does not deny them. He only asks that your thinking mind keep its own boundaries, noticing the feeling without letting it write the plan for the rest of your afternoon.
entries.practice: When a strong bodily feeling arises today, locate it physically before deciding anything.

entries.title: Groan, but Lightly
entries.quote: And I do not say that you are not allowed to groan, but do not groan inwardly; and if your slave is slow in bringing a bandage, do not cry out and torment yourself, and say, Every body hates me; for who would not hate such a man?
entries.reflection: You are allowed to say ouch. A headache or a slow pharmacy line is genuinely unpleasant. The trouble starts when the groan turns inward and becomes a story that everyone is against you. Complaining once is human. Building a case of personal persecution only makes the original discomfort worse.
entries.practice: When something hurts or frustrates you today, mention it once and skip the commentary.

entries.title: Joy Without Clutter
entries.quote: Joy is the goal which you desire to reach, but you are wandering from the path, if you expect to reach your goal while you are in the midst of riches and official titles,—in other words, if you seek joy in the midst of cares. These objects for which you strive so eagerly, as if they would give you happiness and pleasure, are merely causes of grief.
entries.reflection: Plenty of people chase titles, bigger houses, and nicer cars as a route to happiness, then find the new things arrive with new worries attached. Seneca is not against comfort. He simply notices that joy rarely lives inside a pile of cares, and that the things we strive for often deliver anxiety instead.
entries.practice: Write down one goal you are chasing and ask honestly whether it will bring peace.

entries.title: Pain Stops at the Door
entries.quote: Pain is either an evil to the body—then let the body say what it thinks of it—or to the soul; but it is in the power of the soul to maintain its own serenity and tranquillity, and not to think that pain is an evil. For every judgment and movement and desire and aversion is within, and no evil ascends so high.
entries.reflection: A sprained ankle hurts, and Marcus would not pretend otherwise. His point is that the body can register pain while the mind decides what the pain means. Judging it a disaster adds a second injury. Treating it as unpleasant but bearable keeps your mood and your choices in your own hands.
entries.practice: If you feel discomfort today, describe it to yourself in neutral words, without drama.

entries.title: Wanting What Comes
entries.quote: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
entries.reflection: Rain on the picnic, a canceled flight, a meeting that runs long. Most frustration is the gap between the day you planned and the day you got. Epictetus suggests closing that gap from your side, by welcoming what actually happens. It sounds passive, yet it frees enormous energy for what you can still do.
entries.practice: When a plan changes today, say to yourself, this works too, and adjust.

entries.title: Calm Seas, Prepared Mind
entries.quote: He who can bear Fortune, can also beware of Fortune. At any rate, there is no dashing of billows when the sea is calm. And there is nothing more wretched or foolish than premature fear.
entries.reflection: Preparation and panic look similar from a distance, but they feel completely different. Buying insurance, saving an emergency fund, and scheduling the checkup are calm acts of foresight. Lying awake imagining every disaster is not. Seneca wants the first without the second, a quiet sea with a sturdy boat.
entries.practice: Take one sensible precaution you have postponed, then stop worrying about that risk.

entries.title: Counting What You Have
entries.quote: Think not so much of what thou hast not as of what thou hast: but of the things which thou hast select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought, if thou hadst them not. At the same time, however, take care that thou dost not through being so pleased with them accustom thyself to overvalue them, so as to be disturbed if ever thou shouldst not have them.
entries.reflection: An extra day on the calendar is a good moment to take stock. Desire tends to fix on what is missing. Marcus suggests looking at the best of what you already have and imagining how much you would miss it. Just do not cling so tightly that losing it someday would undo you.
entries.practice: List three things you already have that you would badly miss if they vanished.

months.name: March
months.intro: Most of what upsets us is not the event itself but the story we tell about it a half second later. This month is about catching that story in the act: slowing down first impressions, separating what happened from what we added, and learning to see people, things and setbacks a little more truly.

entries.title: The Story We Add
entries.quote: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
entries.reflection: A delayed flight, a curt email, a bad lab result. Each arrives as a plain fact, and within seconds the mind has written a whole verdict about it. That verdict is what keeps you up at night. Noticing the gap between the event and your opinion of it is where steadiness begins, a skill that improves with practice.
entries.practice: When something annoys you today, write the bare fact in one sentence, without adjectives.

entries.title: Remove the Complaint
entries.quote: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
entries.reflection: Harm and the feeling of being harmed are not always the same thing. Someone cuts in line, a colleague takes credit, a relative makes a pointed remark. The sting often lives in the sentence "I have been wronged" that you repeat afterward. Drop the sentence, even for a minute, and see how much of the injury actually remains.
entries.practice: Catch yourself thinking "they did this to me" and replace it with what simply happened.

entries.title: Nothing Unbearable
entries.quote: If you ask me, I think that for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable. I shall not endure myself on that day when I find anything unendurable.
entries.reflection: Calling something unbearable is a decision, and it usually makes the thing heavier. A long commute, a sick child at midnight, a tight month with money: hard, certainly, but most of them are being borne right now by ordinary people. Labeling them differently does not change the facts. It changes how much strength you have left to meet them.
entries.practice: Replace the word "unbearable" with "difficult" every time it comes to mind today.

entries.title: Who Did the Insulting
entries.quote: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you.
entries.reflection: A rude driver or a sharp comment online cannot reach inside your chest. What does the reaching is your own quick judgment that this is an insult and it matters. That sounds like a harsh teaching, yet it is good news. If the irritation is partly yours, then so is the power to set it down.
entries.practice: Before replying to anything that stings, wait ten minutes and ask what you are adding.

entries.title: Things Are Silent
entries.quote: Things stand outside of us, themselves by themselves, neither knowing aught of themselves, nor expressing any judgment. What is it, then, which does judge about them? The ruling faculty.
entries.reflection: Your bank balance does not think it is a disaster. The scale in the bathroom has no opinion about you. Objects and events just sit there, saying nothing. Every bit of meaning they carry is supplied by the mind looking at them, which means the mind is the place worth tending, far more than the numbers.
entries.practice: Look at one number that worries you and say aloud, "This is only a number."

entries.title: The Notion of Loss
entries.quote: Look about you and note the things that drive us mad, which we lose with a flood of tears; you will perceive that it is not the loss that troubles us with reference to these things, but a notion of loss. No one feels that they have been lost, but his mind tells him that it has been so.
entries.reflection: Losing a promotion, a friendship or a favorite watch hurts, but much of the ache comes from replaying what it means. Often the loss is felt for weeks after life has quietly rearranged itself around it. Asking what has actually changed in your day, as opposed to your story, can shrink a grief to its real size.
entries.practice: Name one recent loss and list three things in your day it has not touched.

entries.title: Ask Appearances to Wait
entries.quote: But in the first place, be not hurried away by the rapidity of the appearance, but say, Appearances, wait for me a little; let me see who you are, and what you are about; let me put you to the test.
entries.reflection: First impressions move fast: a notification, a tone of voice, a strange noise from the car. The urge is to react at the same speed. Picture instead asking the impression to hold still for a moment so you can look at it properly. That pause is often the difference between a reply you regret and one you are glad of.
entries.practice: Take three slow breaths before answering any message that makes your pulse jump.

entries.title: What You Actually See
entries.quote: I see that my child is sick. I do see; but that he is in danger, I do not see. Thus then always abide by the first appearances, and add nothing thyself from within, and then nothing happens to thee.
entries.reflection: A fever, a cough, a test that needs repeating. The eyes report something small and real, and the imagination races ahead to the worst ending. Caring well for someone means staying with what is in front of you: the temperature, the next step, the call to make. Fear that runs ahead is no help to anyone you love.
entries.practice: When worry starts, say only what you can see right now, and stop there.

entries.title: Things Lead Us Astray
entries.quote: It is things that lead us astray: it is between things that you must discriminate. We embrace evil instead of good; we pray for something opposite to that which we have prayed for in the past.
entries.reflection: Wordplay rarely ruins a life. What misleads people is the shiny offer, the bigger house, the job title that looks better than it feels. Seneca notices how often we chase something, get it, and then want its opposite. Looking carefully at a thing before wanting it saves a great deal of reversing later.
entries.practice: Before buying anything over fifty dollars today, wait a day and look again.

entries.title: Nothing More Happened
entries.quote: Your ship is lost. What has happened? Your ship is lost. A man has been led to prison. What has happened? He has been led to prison. But that herein he has fared badly, every man adds from his own opinion.
entries.reflection: Epictetus strips events down like a reporter: the ship is lost, the man is in prison, and that is all. The word "badly" is something we bring along ourselves. Try it with a cancelled plan or a rejected proposal. State what happened, then notice the extra commentary trying to attach itself, and leave it off.
entries.practice: Tell someone about a setback today using only facts, with no judgment words.

entries.title: Polish and Persuasion
entries.quote: For outward show is a wonderful perverter of the reason, and when thou art most sure that thou art employed about things worth thy pains, it is then that it cheats thee most.
entries.reflection: Glossy packaging, confident salespeople and beautifully edited photos all work on the same weakness. The moment you feel most certain that something is worth the effort is often the moment you are being sold to. Stripping a thing back to what it really is, ingredients and materials and cost, is a quiet act of self-respect.
entries.practice: Describe one thing you want in plain, unflattering terms before you decide on it.

entries.title: Flattery in Disguise
entries.quote: How closely flattery resembles friendship! It not only apes friendship, but outdoes it, passing it in the race; with wide-open and indulgent ears it is welcomed and sinks to the depths of the heart, and it is pleasing precisely wherein it does harm.
entries.reflection: Praise feels like care, which is exactly why it slips past our defenses. A friend who only agrees, a boss who only compliments, an app that tells you what you want to hear. Real friendship sometimes stings. Learning to tell the two apart is one of the harder kinds of clear sight, and among the most useful.
entries.practice: Ask someone you trust for one honest criticism, and thank them for it.

entries.title: It Seemed Right to Them
entries.quote: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty. It is not possible then for him to follow that which seems right to you, but that which seems right to himself.
entries.reflection: The coworker who undermined you probably believed they were doing the right thing. That does not make them right, yet it changes the picture. They are acting on their view, not yours, and nobody can follow a map they do not have. Seeing this turns a villain back into a mistaken person, which is far easier to live beside.
entries.practice: Think of someone who wronged you and write the reason they likely gave themselves.

entries.title: What Do They Believe
entries.quote: Whatever man thou meetest with, immediately say to thyself: What opinions has this man about good and bad?
entries.reflection: Behavior makes more sense once you know what a person thinks is good. The neighbor obsessed with his lawn, the relative who cannot stop talking about money, the driver weaving through traffic. Each is acting out a belief about what matters. Asking about the belief first makes the behavior far less surprising, and far less personal.
entries.practice: In one conversation today, quietly guess what the other person values most.

entries.title: The Hidden Price
entries.quote: Some objects are superfluous; others are not worth the price we pay for them. But we do not see this clearly, and we regard things as free gifts when they really cost us very dear.
entries.reflection: The free trial, the extra shift, the favor that becomes an obligation. Plenty of things cost no money and still take evenings, sleep and attention. Seneca asks for the kind of scrutiny you would give a car salesman, applied to everything you chase. Time and peace of mind are payment too, and often the most expensive kind.
entries.practice: Pick one commitment and estimate honestly how many hours a month it costs you.

entries.title: Before You Call It Bad
entries.quote: Does a man bathe quickly (early)? do not say that he bathes badly, but that he bathes quickly. Does a man drink much wine? do not say that he does this badly, but say that he drinks much. For before you shall have determined the opinion how do you know whether he is acting wrong?
entries.reflection: He drinks a lot. She left early. They spent heavily. Each is a description, and the word "badly" is a separate claim that needs evidence you usually do not have. Sticking to description is not naive. It keeps you from hanging verdicts on people based on a glimpse through a window, and it keeps gossip from passing as knowledge.
entries.practice: Describe someone's behavior today without adding whether it was good or bad.

entries.title: The Healthy Eye
entries.quote: The healthy eye ought to see all visible things and not to say, I wish for green things; for this is the condition of a diseased eye.
entries.reflection: An eye that only wants green is a sick eye. In the same way, a mind that only accepts good news, smooth days and agreeable people is fragile. Seeing clearly includes seeing the traffic, the bill, the tired spouse and the cancelled plans, and taking them in without demanding that the world show only its pleasant side.
entries.practice: When unwelcome news arrives, say "noted" before you say anything else.

entries.title: The Only Real Trouble
entries.quote: Spite of all do you still chafe and complain, not understanding that, in all the evils to which you refer, there is really only one—the fact that you do chafe and complain?
entries.reflection: Seneca makes a bold claim: of all a friend's troubles, the one real problem is the complaining. That can sound unkind, yet consider how much of a hard week is spent rehearsing its unfairness. The leaky roof is a task. The endless grumbling about it is a second burden that you carry by choice.
entries.practice: Go one full day without complaining aloud, and notice when you nearly do.

entries.title: Seeming Is Not Being
entries.quote: What then “seems” to every man is not sufficient for determining what “is”; for neither in the case of weights nor measures are we satisfied with the bare appearance, but in each case we have discovered a certain rule.
entries.reflection: Nobody weighs groceries by feel or measures a room by eye when it matters. Yet people judge right and wrong, success and failure, mostly by how things seem in the moment. A strong feeling of certainty is not the same as being correct. It helps to have a standard outside your mood, something steady you can check a feeling against.
entries.practice: Write down one firm opinion you hold and the evidence that would change it.

entries.title: Not Their Version
entries.quote: Do not have such an opinion of things as he has who does thee wrong, or such as he wishes thee to have, but look at them as they are in truth.
entries.reflection: Someone who has hurt you would often like you to see things their way: that you overreacted, that it was your fault, that you are small. You do not have to accept their framing, and you do not have to invent a harsher one in reply. The task is simply to look at what actually happened.
entries.practice: After a conflict, write one sentence of what happened as a neutral witness would.

entries.title: Vices in Good Clothes
entries.quote: Vices creep into our hearts under the name of virtues, rashness lurks beneath the appellation of bravery, moderation is called sluggishness, and the coward is regarded as prudent; there is great danger if we go astray in these matters.
entries.reflection: Recklessness calls itself courage. Stinginess calls itself being careful. Overwork calls itself dedication, and avoiding a hard talk calls itself keeping the peace. The labels feel flattering, which is why they stick. Checking what a habit really is, under its nicer name, is uncomfortable and worth doing.
entries.practice: Name one habit you praise in yourself and ask what a blunt friend would call it.

entries.title: Do Not Follow the Picture
entries.quote: And then do not allow the appearance to lead you on and draw lively pictures of the things which will follow; for if you do, it will carry you off wherever it pleases. But rather bring in to oppose it some other beautiful and noble appearance, and cast out this base appearance.
entries.reflection: One craving or worry quickly becomes a movie: the late-night snack becomes the whole bag, the odd pain becomes a hospital stay, the unanswered text becomes a ruined friendship. The trick is to stop the reel early and put a better image in its place before the story takes you somewhere you did not choose.
entries.practice: When a worry starts spinning a story, picture instead the most likely ordinary outcome.

entries.title: Why Am I Disturbed
entries.quote: I can have that opinion about anything which I ought to have. If I can, why am I disturbed?
entries.reflection: Marcus asks himself a blunt question. If he can choose the view he takes of things, why is he upset? It is a useful question in a traffic jam or a tense meeting. Sometimes the honest answer is that you have not yet chosen, and the first view on offer simply moved in.
entries.practice: Next time you feel rattled, ask yourself, "Which opinion am I holding right now?"

entries.title: Too Soon to Tell
entries.quote: Has that friend of yours already made you believe that he is a good man? And yet it is impossible in so short a time for one either to become good or be known as such.
entries.reflection: A charming new colleague, a contractor who says all the right things, a first date that goes perfectly. Quick verdicts about people are tempting, in both directions. Character shows itself slowly, through small choices over months. Holding first impressions loosely protects you from both disappointment and unfair dislike.
entries.practice: Think of someone you judged quickly this year, and ask what you actually know.

entries.title: How You Will Fare
entries.quote: But if you ask me how you will fare, I can tell you: if you have right opinions, you will fare well; if they are false, you will fare ill. For to every man the cause of his acting is opinion.
entries.reflection: Nobody can promise how the lawsuit, the interview or the diagnosis will turn out. What can be said is that sound beliefs tend to lead to sound choices, and confused ones lead to trouble. Tending to your opinions is less dramatic than chasing outcomes, but it is the part that travels with you into every result.
entries.practice: Before a big decision, write the belief driving it and test whether it holds up.

entries.title: Glad to Be Corrected
entries.quote: If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured. But he is injured who abides in his error and ignorance.
entries.reflection: Being shown you were wrong feels like a small defeat, especially in front of family or coworkers. Marcus treats it as a gift. The truth never harmed anyone; clinging to an error does. Picture arguing with your spouse or a colleague with real willingness to change your mind, and how much lighter that would feel.
entries.practice: In your next disagreement, ask "What am I missing?" and listen to the full answer.

entries.title: Dust on the Road
entries.quote: But come, did you not know, when you prayed for long life, that this was what you were praying for? A long life includes all these troubles, just as a long journey includes dust and mud and rain.
entries.reflection: Hoping for a long life and then resenting aches, illness and loss is a bit like booking a road trip and being shocked by the dust. The troubles are part of the package. Seeing that plainly does not make them pleasant, but it removes the extra sting of feeling ambushed by something that was always coming.
entries.practice: When an age-related ache shows up today, say "part of the trip" and carry on.

entries.title: The Storm Inside
entries.quote: For what is a greater storm than that which comes from appearances which are violent and drive away the reason? For the storm itself, what else is it but an appearance?
entries.reflection: The real storm is often the one in your head: a spiral of alarming impressions that blows reason away. A tense diagnosis or a sudden layoff is hard enough. The panic layered on top makes clear thinking nearly impossible. Recognizing panic as appearances, not facts, gives you something solid to stand on until the weather passes.
entries.practice: When panic rises, name it out loud as "a storm of impressions" and breathe slowly.

entries.title: You Go to Them
entries.quote: If the things do not come to thee, the pursuits and avoidances of which disturb thee, still in a manner thou goest to them. Let then thy judgment about them be at rest, and they will remain quiet, and thou wilt not be seen either pursuing or avoiding.
entries.reflection: Many of the things that unsettle you are not in the room at all. A rival's success, a news story, a purchase you cannot afford. You travel to them in thought, again and again. Letting your judgment about them settle means they can stay where they are, and you can stay where you are.
entries.practice: When your mind drifts to a distant worry, bring attention back to your hands.

entries.title: Rich by Wanting Less
entries.quote: It is in the power of any man to despise all things, but of no man to possess all things. The shortest cut to riches is to despise riches.
entries.reflection: Nobody can own everything, yet anyone can stop treating every object as a need. The next phone, the nicer car, the bigger kitchen keep moving out of reach. Seeing them clearly, as pleasant extras rather than requirements, is a kind of wealth no market can take away, and it costs nothing to start.
entries.practice: Unsubscribe from one shopping email or app that keeps telling you what you lack.

entries.title: Trouble Cast Out
entries.quote: To-day I have got out of all trouble, or rather I have cast out all trouble, for it was not outside, but within and in my opinions.
entries.reflection: Marcus does not say his problems vanished. He says he threw out the trouble, because it was living in his opinions all along. That is the point of a month spent looking carefully. The facts of your life may be the same tonight, while the weight you carry on top of them can be a good deal lighter.
entries.practice: Tonight, list one worry you dropped this month simply by seeing it differently.

months.name: April
months.theme: The Work in Front of You
months.intro: Most days are not made of grand decisions. They are made of the next email, the next patient, the next load of laundry, the next honest hour at the desk. This month is about getting up, turning toward the task that is actually yours, and doing it well without waiting to feel ready.

entries.title: Out From Under the Covers
entries.quote: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,—I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world?
entries.reflection: The alarm goes off and the bed argues its case. Marcus had the same argument with himself, and he answered it by naming what the day was for. You are not getting up to endure a schedule. You are getting up to be useful to the people and tasks waiting on you, which is exactly the point of being here.
entries.practice: Before checking your phone, say aloud the one piece of work today is for.

entries.title: Know What You Are Starting
entries.quote: When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is.
entries.reflection: A school pickup line, a budget meeting, a family dinner with a difficult relative: each has its usual friction. Naming that friction before you walk in keeps it from ambushing you. Expecting the interruptions, the delays and the snide comment lets you keep your temper and your aim while everyone else is surprised.
entries.practice: Before your hardest appointment today, list two annoyances likely to happen there.

entries.title: Take the Hill
entries.quote: Rise, draw a fresh breath, and surmount that hill, if possible, at a single spurt!" Work is the sustenance of noble minds.
entries.reflection: Seneca writes like a coach on the sideline, shouting encouragement to a runner who is tired but still moving. Effort toward something worthwhile is not a punishment to get through. It feeds you. The report you finally finish, the run you did not skip, leave you stronger than the evening you spent avoiding them.
entries.practice: Pick the task you have postponed longest and give it twenty unbroken minutes.

entries.title: Whatever the Weather
entries.quote: Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty; and whether thou art drowsy or satisfied with sleep; and whether ill-spoken of or praised; and whether dying or doing something else.
entries.reflection: Tired, chilly, underslept, criticized, praised: none of these changes what the job requires. A nurse on a night shift and a parent up with a sick toddler both know this. Conditions will rarely be ideal, and the work is still waiting. Comfort is pleasant when it comes, but it was never part of the job description.
entries.practice: Notice one complaint about conditions today and do the task without voicing it.

entries.title: Count the Cost First
entries.quote: In every act consider what precedes and what follows, and then proceed to the act.
entries.reflection: Plenty of gym memberships, side businesses and language apps begin with enthusiasm and end in quiet abandonment. Thinking through what a commitment will really demand, the early mornings and the boring middle, is not pessimism. It is how you choose things you will actually finish instead of things you merely admire.
entries.practice: Write down what your current goal will cost you each week, honestly.

entries.title: Life in Little Bits
entries.quote: And much harm is done even by one who holds you back, especially since life is so short; and we make it still shorter by our unsteadiness, by making ever fresh beginnings at life, now one and immediately another. We break up life into little bits, and fritter it away.
entries.reflection: Every new plan feels like progress, which is why starting over is so tempting. A fresh notebook, a new system, a different diet: each one resets the clock to zero. Steady people are not more talented. They simply keep building on yesterday instead of tearing it down and laying a new foundation every Monday.
entries.practice: Return to one abandoned project and do the next step instead of redesigning it.

entries.title: Not Ten Thousand Years
entries.quote: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
entries.reflection: Someday is a comfortable word. Someday you will call your brother, fix the gutter, read to the kids more, start saving properly. Marcus reminds himself that the supply of days is limited and unknown. That is not meant to frighten you. It is meant to move the good thing from someday onto today's list.
entries.practice: Take one item from your someday list and schedule it for this week.

entries.title: Play the Part Well
entries.quote: Remember that thou art an actor in a play, of such a kind as the teacher (author) may choose; if short, of a short one; if long, of a long one: if he wishes you to act the part of a poor man, see that you act the part naturally; if the part of a lame man, of a magistrate, of a private person, (do the same). For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
entries.reflection: Nobody picked their parents, their height, their hometown or the economy they graduated into. You can spend energy resenting the role or spend it performing the role with skill and grace. The person caring for an aging parent, or working an unglamorous job, can still play it beautifully.
entries.practice: Name your least favorite role this week and do one part of it wholeheartedly.

entries.title: Ask for the Work
entries.quote: I forbid you to be cast down or depressed. It is not enough if you do not shrink from work; ask for it.
entries.reflection: There is a difference between tolerating hard tasks and seeking them. Volunteering for the tricky project, taking the shift no one wants, offering to handle the paperwork: these build the kind of capacity that cannot be gained by waiting. Discouragement fades faster when your hands are busy with something difficult and worthwhile.
entries.practice: Volunteer today for one task others are avoiding, at work or at home.

entries.title: Neither Martyr Nor Star
entries.quote: Labor not as one who is wretched, nor yet as one who would be pitied or admired; but direct thy will to one thing only—to put thyself in motion and to check thyself, as the social reason requires.
entries.reflection: Some people work while sighing loudly so everyone knows how hard it is. Others work for the applause. Both are performing for an audience. Marcus wants something quieter: do the work because it needs doing, start when it is time, stop when it is enough, and let nobody's pity or praise set the pace.
entries.practice: Finish one chore today without mentioning it to anyone afterward.

entries.title: What Can I Use Here
entries.quote: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use.
entries.reflection: A canceled flight, a rude reply, a back that aches on the drive home. Each one arrives with a question attached: what in me can meet this? Sometimes the answer is patience, sometimes endurance, sometimes a sense of humor. Asking the question shifts you from victim of the moment to someone with tools in hand.
entries.practice: When something goes wrong today, name the specific strength it is asking you to use.

entries.title: The Same Wants as Yesterday
entries.quote: Make progress, and, before all else, endeavour to be consistent with yourself. And when you would find out whether you have accomplished anything, consider whether you desire the same things to-day that you desired yesterday.
entries.reflection: Here is a simple test of whether you are getting anywhere. Are you still pursuing what you chose last week, or has a new podcast, ad or friend's success pulled you off in another direction? Wanting different things every few days feels lively but usually means drifting. Steady aims are what let small efforts add up.
entries.practice: Compare today's priorities with last month's and drop one that does not belong.

entries.title: Am I Up to This
entries.quote: Is my understanding sufficient for this or not? If it is sufficient, I use it for the work as an instrument given by the universal nature.
entries.reflection: An honest question lies underneath every assignment: do I have what this needs? If yes, use it fully, without false modesty. If not, the answer is not to bluff. Ask a colleague, hand it to someone better suited, or learn what you are missing. Knowing your capacity is part of doing work well.
entries.practice: Before your next task, ask whether you are the right person, and act on the answer.

entries.title: Whole Soul, One Thing
entries.quote: So you also do: you are at one time a wrestler (athlete), then a gladiator, then a philosopher, then a rhetorician; but with your whole soul you are nothing: like the ape you imitate all that you see; and always one thing after another pleases you, but that which becomes familiar displeases you.
entries.reflection: Scroll long enough and every life looks appealing: the woodworker, the marathoner, the startup founder, the homesteader. Trying on each identity for a week leaves you with a closet of costumes and no real craft. Choosing one path and staying through the dull parts is where actual skill and satisfaction live.
entries.practice: Unfollow three accounts that pull you toward hobbies you will never actually pursue.

entries.title: Use It or Lose It
entries.quote: Our luxuries have condemned us to weakness; we have ceased to be able to do that which we have long declined to do.
entries.reflection: Elevators, delivery apps and autocomplete save effort, and that is mostly good. But every ability left unused quietly shrinks: walking, cooking, writing a full paragraph, fixing something yourself. Seneca noticed this after being carried around in comfort. A little chosen effort each day keeps you able to do what life will eventually demand.
entries.practice: Do one thing by hand today that you would normally outsource or automate.

entries.title: No Shame in Help
entries.quote: Be not ashamed to be helped; for it is thy business to do thy duty like a soldier in the assault on a town. How then, if being lame thou canst not mount up on the battlements alone, but with the help of another it is possible?
entries.reflection: Pride often dresses up as independence. You struggle alone with the spreadsheet, the heavy couch, the diagnosis you do not understand, because asking feels like failing. But the goal was always to get the job done, not to prove you could do it alone. A boost over the wall still gets you over the wall.
entries.practice: Ask one person for help with something you have been stubbornly handling alone.

entries.title: Eat as You Ought
entries.quote: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems (philosophical rules, precepts); but do that which follows from them. For example, at a banquet do not say how a man ought to eat, but eat as you ought to eat.
entries.reflection: Talking about good habits is easy and oddly satisfying. Explaining nutrition at a barbecue, sharing productivity tips, posting about mindfulness. Epictetus would rather you simply eat well, work well and stay calm, and let the results speak. Lecturing others often replaces the practice instead of reflecting it.
entries.practice: Keep one good habit today entirely to yourself, with no mention or post.

entries.title: Built for the Struggle
entries.quote: You may be sure that this refractory nature, which demands much toil, has been implanted in us. There are obstacles in our path; so let us fight, and call to our assistance some helpers.
entries.reflection: If self-discipline feels harder for you than for others, you are not broken. Seneca assumes resistance is built in and plans for it. The answer is not to wait for the struggle to vanish but to recruit allies: a workout partner, a mentor, a friend who checks in. Obstacles are expected, and so is help.
entries.practice: Text someone and ask them to check on one commitment you made this week.

entries.title: On Purpose
entries.quote: First, do nothing inconsiderately, nor without a purpose. Second, make thy acts refer to nothing else than to a social end.
entries.reflection: So much of a day happens on autopilot: opening apps, wandering into the kitchen, saying yes to meetings. Two short rules cover a lot. Know why you are doing a thing, and let that reason include other people. Even routine tasks change character when they are chosen deliberately and done with someone else in mind.
entries.practice: Before opening any app today, pause and name your reason for opening it.

entries.title: Your Side of the Relationship
entries.quote: Does a brother wrong you? Maintain then your own position towards him, and do not examine what he is doing, but what you must do that your will shall be conformable to nature.
entries.reflection: When a sibling, coworker or ex behaves badly, the instinct is to audit their every move. That audit never ends and changes nothing. Epictetus redirects your attention to your own conduct: what does a good brother, colleague or co-parent do here? That question has an answer you can actually carry out.
entries.practice: In one strained relationship, decide your next decent action without reviewing their faults.

entries.title: Finish What You Laid Out
entries.quote: I would not have you greater or better than you planned; for in your case the mere foundations have covered a large extent of ground; only finish all that you have laid out, and take in hand the plans which you have had in mind.
entries.reflection: You may not need bigger goals. You may need to complete the ones already sketched: the half-renovated bathroom, the course you paid for, the savings plan you set up and ignored. Seneca tells his friend the foundations are already wide enough. The task now is building on them, not drawing new blueprints.
entries.practice: Choose one unfinished plan and write the three steps that would complete it.

entries.title: One Act at a Time
entries.quote: It is thy duty to order thy life well in every single act; and if every act does its duty as far as is possible, be content; and no one is able to hinder thee so that each act shall not do its duty.—But something external will stand in the way. Nothing will stand in the way of thy acting justly and soberly and considerately.—But perhaps some other active power will be hindered.
entries.reflection: A whole well-lived life is too big to manage, but the next conversation or task is not. Marcus breaks it down to single acts and notices that no one can stop you from doing the current one fairly and carefully. A delay or a setback may change what you do, never how well you do it.
entries.practice: When a plan gets blocked today, ask what the best available next act is.

entries.title: This I Can Do
entries.quote: This power I possess; this I can do. But the rest I do not possess, nor can I do.
entries.reflection: Short and plain, this is a useful sorting tool for an overloaded mind. Some things on your plate are fully in your hands: your effort, your honesty, your tone. Others, like the test results or the market, simply are not. Pour yourself into the first pile and stop wearing yourself out on the second.
entries.practice: Split your worry list into two columns and act on one item from the first.

entries.title: Keep the Faith
entries.quote: I do not know whether I shall make progress; but I should prefer to lack success rather than to lack faith.
entries.reflection: Seneca is trying to help a friend change, and he has no guarantee it will work. He tries anyway.
